paragraphs: “What promotion?”
“His elder stinks.”

“What? That’s nonsense, you just want to say something nasty. Shut up, you fool! Let me sit on your knee, Alyosha, like this.” She suddenly skipped forward and hopped onto his knee, laughing, like a kitten, with her right arm around his neck. “I’ll cheer you up, my pious boy. Really, will you let me sit here? You won’t be angry? Tell me, and I’ll get off.”

Alyosha said nothing. He sat there afraid to move. He heard her words, “Tell me, and I’ll get off,” but he did not answer. Still, nothing stirred in his heart of what Rakitin, say, watching him spitefully from his corner, might have expected or imagined. His great grief swallowed every feeling that might have been roused. If he had been able to think clearly just then, he would have seen that he was wearing the strongest armor against every lust and temptation. Yet, dazed as he was and crushed by sorrow, he could not help noticing a new and strange feeling in his heart. This woman, this “dreadful” woman, did not frighten him now. He felt none of the fear that used to rise in his soul whenever a thought of any woman crossed his mind. Quite the opposite. This was the woman he had feared more than any other, and she was sitting on his knee with her arms around him. She woke in him a different, unexpected, odd feeling: the keenest, purest interest, with no trace of his old terror. That was what surprised him, though he could not have said why.
“You’ve talked enough nonsense,” cried Rakitin. “You’d be better off giving us some champagne. You owe it to me, and you know it!”

“Yes, I do. Do you know, Alyosha, on top of everything else I promised him champagne if he’d bring you here? I’ll have some too! Fenya, Fenya, bring the bottle Mitya left! Be quick! I’m stingy, but I’ll stand you a bottle anyway. Not for you, Rakitin, you’re a toadstool, but he’s a falcon! My heart is full of something very different, but never mind, I’ll drink with you. I feel like letting myself go.”
“But what’s wrong with you? And what is this message, if I may ask? Or is it a secret?” Rakitin put in, curious, doing his best to look as if he hadn’t noticed the snubs that kept coming his way.

“Ech, it’s no secret, and you know it,” Grushenka said, her voice suddenly anxious. She turned toward Rakitin and drew a little away from Alyosha, though she still sat on his knee with her arm around his neck. “My officer is coming, Rakitin. My officer is coming.”
“I heard he was coming, but is he that close already?”
“He’s at Mokroe now. He’ll send a messenger from there, he wrote. I got his letter today. I’m expecting the messenger any minute.”
“You don’t say! Why Mokroe?”
“That’s a long story. I’ve told you enough.”
“Mitya will be up to something now! Tell me, does he know or doesn’t he?”

“Does he know! Of course not. If he knew, there’d be murder. But I’m not afraid of that now, I’m not afraid of his knife. Quiet, Rakitin, don’t remind me of Dmitri Fyodorovitch. He’s bruised my heart. I don’t want to think about that right now. I can think about Alyosha, I can look at Alyosha ... smile at me, dear, cheer up, smile at my silliness, at my happiness.... Ah, he’s smiling, he’s smiling! How kindly he looks at me! And you know, Alyosha, all this time I’ve been thinking you were angry with me about the day before yesterday, about that young lady. I behaved like a cur, that’s the truth.... But it’s good that it happened. It was horrid, but good as well.” Grushenka smiled dreamily, and a faintly cruel line showed in her smile. “Mitya told me she screamed that I ‘ought to be flogged.’ I did insult her terribly. She sent for me, she wanted to win me over, to bribe me with her chocolate.... No, it’s good that it ended like that.” She smiled again. “But I’m still afraid you’re angry with me.”
“Well, that’s really true,” Rakitin put in suddenly, genuinely surprised. “Alyosha, she’s honestly afraid of a chicken like you.”
“He’s a chicken to you, Rakitin ... because you have no conscience, that’s why! You see, I love him with my whole soul, that’s how it is! Alyosha, do you believe I love you with my whole soul?”
“Ah, you shameless woman! She’s declaring herself to you, Alexey!”
“So what? I love him!”
“And your officer? And the priceless message from Mokroe?”
“That’s something else entirely.”
“Typical woman!”

“Don’t make me angry, Rakitin.” Grushenka cut in hotly. “It’s something else entirely. I love Alyosha in another way. It’s true, Alyosha, I had sly plans for you once. I’m a horrid, violent creature. But at other times I’ve looked at you, Alyosha, as my conscience. I kept thinking, ‘How someone like him must despise a nasty thing like me.’ I thought that the day before yesterday, running home from the young lady’s. I’ve thought of you this way for a long time, Alyosha, and Mitya knows, I’ve talked to him about it. Mitya understands. Believe it or not, there are times I look at you and feel ashamed, completely ashamed of myself.... How and since when I started thinking of you like this, I can’t say, I don’t remember....”
Fenya came in and set a tray on the table, with an open bottle and three glasses of champagne.

“The champagne!” cried Rakitin. “You’re worked up, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you’re not yourself. One glass of champagne and you’ll be ready to dance. Eh, they can’t even manage this properly,” he added, looking at the bottle. “The old woman poured it in the kitchen, and the bottle’s come in warm, with no cork. Well, give me some anyway.”
He went to the table, took a glass, drank it off in one gulp and poured himself another.

“You don’t often come across champagne,” he said, licking his lips. “Now, Alyosha, take a glass, show us what you’re made of! What shall we drink to? The gates of paradise? Take a glass, Grushenka, you drink to the gates of paradise too.”
“What gates of paradise?”
She took a glass. Alyosha took his, sipped it and put it down.
“No, I’d rather not,” he said with a gentle smile.
“And you bragged!” cried Rakitin.
“Then I won’t either,” chimed in Grushenka. “I don’t really want any. You can drink the whole bottle alone, Rakitin. If Alyosha drinks, I will.”

“How touching and sentimental!” said Rakitin with a sneer. “And she’s sitting on his knee, too! He has something to grieve over, but what’s your excuse? He’s rebelling against his God and ready to eat sausage....”
“What do you mean?”
“His elder died today. Father Zossima, the saint.”

“So Father Zossima is dead,” cried Grushenka. “Good God, I didn’t know!” She crossed herself devoutly. “Heavens, what am I doing, sitting on his knee like this at a time like this!” She jumped up as if in alarm, slipped off his knee at once and sat down on the sofa.
Alyosha looked at her for a long time, wondering, and a light seemed to dawn on his face.

“Rakitin,” he said suddenly, in a firm, loud voice, “don’t taunt me that I’ve rebelled against God. I don’t want to be angry with you, so be kinder yourself. I’ve lost a treasure that you’ve never had, and you can’t judge me now. Look at her instead. Do you see how she pities me? I came here looking for a wicked soul. I was drawn to evil because I was base and evil myself. And I’ve found a true sister, I’ve found a treasure, a loving heart. She pitied me just now.... Agrafena Alexandrovna, I’m speaking of you. You’ve lifted my soul out of the depths.”
Alyosha’s lips were trembling, and he was catching his breath.
“So she’s saved you, it seems,” laughed Rakitin spitefully. “And she meant to get you in her clutches, you know that?”

“Wait, Rakitin.” Grushenka sprang up. “Quiet, both of you. Now I’ll tell you everything. Quiet, Alyosha, your words shame me, because I’m bad, not good. That’s what I am. And you be quiet, Rakitin, because you’re lying. It’s true that I had the low idea of getting him into my clutches, but now you’re lying, now everything is different. I don’t want to hear another word from you, Rakitin.”
Grushenka said all this in great agitation.
“They’re both crazy,” said Rakitin, staring at them in amazement. “I feel like I’m in a madhouse. They’re both going so soft that they’ll start crying in a minute.”
“I will cry, I will,” repeated Grushenka. “He called me his sister, and I’ll never forget it. But let me tell you, Rakitin, bad as I am, I did give away an onion.”
“An onion? Damn it, you really are crazy.”

Rakitin was amazed at their heat. He was hurt and annoyed, though he might have considered that each of them was passing through a crisis of the soul, the kind that doesn’t come often in a lifetime. But Rakitin was touchy about anything that concerned himself and very thick-skinned about what other people felt. That came partly from his youth and inexperience, and partly from his enormous egoism.

“You see, Alyosha,” Grushenka said, turning to him with a nervous laugh, “I was bragging when I told Rakitin I’d given away an onion. I’m not telling you to brag. It’s just a story, but it’s a nice one. I heard it as a child from Matryona, my cook, who still works for me. It goes like this. Once there was a peasant woman, and a very wicked woman she was. She died without leaving a single good deed behind her. The devils seized her and threw her into the lake of fire. Her guardian angel stood by, wondering what good deed of hers he could remember to tell God. ‘She pulled up an onion once in her garden,’ he said, ‘and gave it to a beggar woman.’ And God answered: ‘Take that onion, then, and hold it out to her in the lake. Let her take hold and be pulled out. If you can pull her out of the lake, she may come to Paradise. But if the onion breaks, she must stay where she is.’ The angel ran to the woman and held the onion out to her. ‘Here,’ he said, ‘take hold, and I’ll pull you out.’ And he began pulling her out, carefully. He had just got her all the way out when the other sinners in the lake saw her being pulled up, and began grabbing at her to be pulled out too. But she was a very wicked woman, and she began kicking them. ‘I’m the one being pulled out, not you. It’s my onion, not yours.’ The moment she said it, the onion broke. The woman fell back into the lake, and she’s burning there to this day. So the angel wept and went away. That’s the story, Alyosha. I know it by heart, because I’m that wicked woman myself. I bragged to Rakitin that I’d given away an onion, but to you I’ll say: ‘All my life I’ve done nothing but give away one onion, that’s the only good deed I’ve ever done.’ So don’t praise me, Alyosha, don’t think I’m good. I’m bad, I’m a wicked woman, and you make me ashamed if you praise me. Eh, I have to confess everything. Listen, Alyosha. I wanted so badly to get hold of you that I promised Rakitin twenty-five roubles if he’d bring you to me. Wait, Rakitin, stay where you are!”
She went briskly to the table, opened a drawer, took out a purse and drew a twenty-five rouble note from it.
“What nonsense! What nonsense!” cried Rakitin, thrown off balance.
“Take it. I owe it to you, Rakitin. I know you won’t refuse it, you asked for it yourself.” And she tossed the note to him.
“As if I’d refuse,” boomed Rakitin, plainly embarrassed but covering it with a swagger. “It will come in very handy. Fools exist for the profit of wise men.”
“And now keep your mouth shut, Rakitin. What I’m going to say is not for your ears. Sit in that corner and be quiet. You don’t like us, so hold your tongue.”

“Why would I like you?” Rakitin snarled, making no effort to hide his bad temper. He put the twenty-five rouble note in his pocket, ashamed that Alyosha had seen it. He had counted on being paid later, without Alyosha knowing, and now, feeling ashamed, he lost his temper. Until then he had thought it wise not to contradict Grushenka too bluntly, despite her snubs, since he wanted something out of her. But now he was angry too.
“You love people for a reason. But what have either of you ever done for me?”
“You should love people for no reason, the way Alyosha does.”
“How does he love you? What has he done to show it, that you make such a fuss?”
Grushenka stood in the middle of the room. She spoke heatedly, and her voice had a hysterical edge.

“Be quiet, Rakitin, you know nothing about us! And don’t you dare talk to me like that again. How dare you be so familiar! Sit in that corner and keep quiet, as if you were my footman! And now, Alyosha, I’ll tell you the whole truth, so you can see what a wretch I am! I’m not talking to Rakitin, I’m talking to you. I wanted to ruin you, Alyosha, that’s the holy truth. I was fully set on it. I wanted it so badly that I bribed Rakitin to bring you. And why did I want to do such a thing? You knew nothing about it, Alyosha. You turned away from me, and when you passed me you lowered your eyes. I’d looked at you a hundred times before today. I started asking everybody about you. Your face haunted my heart. ‘He despises me,’ I thought, ‘he won’t even look at me.’ In the end it hurt so much that I was amazed at myself, being so afraid of a boy. I’ll get him in my clutches and laugh at him, I thought. I was full of spite and anger. Believe me, nobody here dares to speak, or even think, of coming to Agrafena Alexandrovna with any bad intention. Old Kuzma is the only man I have anything to do with here. I was bound and sold to him. Satan brought us together, but there’s been no one else. But looking at you, I thought, I’ll get him in my clutches and laugh at him. You see what a spiteful cur I am, and you called me your sister! And now the man who wronged me has come. I’m sitting here waiting for word from him. And do you know what that man has been to me? Five years ago, when Kuzma brought me here, I used to lock myself in so nobody could see or hear me. I was a silly slip of a girl. I used to sit here sobbing. I used to lie awake all night thinking: ‘Where is he now, the man who wronged me? He’s laughing at me with some other woman, I bet. If only I could see him, if I could meet him again, I’d pay him back, I’d pay him back!’ At night I’d lie in the dark sobbing into my pillow, brooding over it. I used to tear at my own heart on purpose and gloat over my anger. ‘I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back!’ That’s what I’d cry out in the dark. And when I suddenly thought that really I would do nothing to him, and that he was laughing at me then, or maybe had forgotten me completely, I’d throw myself on the floor, break down in helpless tears, and lie there shaking until dawn. In the morning I’d get up meaner than a dog, ready to tear the whole world to pieces. And then what do you think? I started saving money, I grew hard-hearted, I got stout. Wiser, would you say? No, nobody in the whole world sees it, nobody knows it. But when night comes, I sometimes lie just as I did five years ago, when I was a silly girl, clenching my teeth and crying all night, thinking, ‘I’ll pay him back, I’ll pay him back!’ Do you hear? Well, now you understand me. A month ago a letter came. He was coming, he was a widower, he wanted to see me. It took my breath away. Then I suddenly thought: ‘If he comes and whistles for me, I’ll crawl back to him like a beaten dog.’ I couldn’t believe it of myself. Am I really so low? Will I run to him or not? I’ve been in such a rage with myself all this month that I’m worse than I was five years ago. Do you see now, Alyosha, what a violent, vengeful creature I am? I’ve told you the whole truth! I played with Mitya to keep myself from running to that other man. Quiet, Rakitin, it’s not for you to judge me, I’m not speaking to you. Before you came in, I was lying here waiting, brooding, deciding my whole life to come, and you can never know what was in my heart. Yes, Alyosha, tell your young lady not to be angry with me for what happened the day before yesterday.... Nobody in the whole world knows what I’m going through now, and nobody ever can know.... Because maybe I’ll take a knife with me today, I can’t make up my mind ...”
